notes.front: What is skin effect?
notes.back: The flow of alternating current near the surface of a conductor at radio frequencies.
notes.explanation: The name describes it: at RF the current keeps to the conductor's outer skin instead of using the whole wire.
notes.example: Like a crowd pressed against the walls of a hall, leaving the middle empty: at RF the centre of a thick wire carries very little.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, glossary, "skin effect", p. AI-9
notes.evidence: SKIN EFFECT—The flow of ac current near the surface of a conductor at rf frequencies.

notes.front: What is reactive power?
notes.back: Power that coils and capacitors take from the source and then return to it, so none of it is used up.
notes.explanation: As a coil's field builds it takes power; as the field collapses it gives the power back, so the power flows to and fro.
notes.example: Like lending a neighbour a ladder every morning and getting it back each evening: it keeps moving, but none is used up.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 2, chapter 4, power in AC circuits, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: the field collapses and returns the power to the source. You can see therefore that no power is used up in either case, since the power alternately flows to and from the source. This power that is returned to the source by the reactive components in the circuit is called REACTIVE POWER.

notes.front: What is real power (called true power in the Navy course)?
notes.back: The power actually used in a circuit, measured in watts: the power in the circuit's resistance.
notes.explanation: To work it out, use the voltage and current that belong to the resistance, not those of the whole circuit.
notes.example: Like the fuel a car actually burns: a 10-ohm resistor carrying 2 A uses 2² × 10 = 40 W, whatever reactance sits beside it.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 2, chapter 4, calculating true power, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: the true power of a circuit is the power actually used in the circuit. This power, measured in watts, is the power associated with the total resistance in the circuit. To calculate true power, the voltage and current associated with the resistance must be used.

notes.front: What is parasitic reactance?
notes.back: Reactance a real component has besides its nominal (intended) reactance; the nominal and parasitic reactance together create its self-resonance.
notes.explanation: Because every real part carries some parasitic reactance, each has a frequency at which it resonates on its own.
notes.example: Like a capacitor that also acts a little like a coil: an electrolytic's parasitic inductance makes it unsuitable at RF.
notes.evidence: E5D07 (B) What combines to create the self-resonance of a component? A. The component’s resistance and reactance B. The component’s nominal and parasitic reactance

notes.front: What is inter-turn capacitance in an inductor?
notes.back: Capacitance between a coil's turns: the parasitic characteristic that creates an inductor's self-resonance.
notes.explanation: It is capacitance the coil was never meant to have, which is why the pool calls it a parasitic characteristic.
notes.example: Like tiny capacitors hidden between neighbouring turns of wire on a coil former.
notes.evidence: E5D06 (D) What parasitic characteristic creates an inductor’s self-resonance? A. Skin effect B. Dielectric loss C. Coupling D. Inter-turn capacitance

notes.front: What is the electrical length of a line?
notes.back: Its length measured against the wavelength it carries: electrically long when long compared with a quarter-wavelength.
notes.explanation: Short and long are relative: the same piece of line can be electrically short at one frequency and long at another.
notes.example: Like a garden path: a short stroll for a person but a long trek for an ant. A 1-metre lead is short at HF but long at 10 GHz.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 3, length of a transmission line, p. 3-9
notes.evidence: A transmission line is electrically long when its physical length is long compared to a quarter- wavelength of the energy it is to carry. You must understand that the terms "short" and "long" are relative ones.

notes.front: In a wire carrying alternating current, what slows the movement of electrons in the centre?
notes.back: Self-induction: the expanding and collapsing fields around each electron encircle other electrons and retard them.
notes.explanation: This is where skin effect begins; with DC, by contrast, the movement of electrons across the wire is uniform.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 3, copper losses, p. 3-7
notes.evidence: When dc flows through a conductor, the movement of electrons through the conductor's cross section is uniform. The situation is somewhat different when ac is applied. The expanding and collapsing fields about each electron encircle other electrons. This phenomenon, called SELF INDUCTION, retards the movement of the encircled electrons.

notes.front: Why does a conductor's resistance rise with frequency because of skin effect?
notes.back: The effective cross-sectional area shrinks as frequency rises, and resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area.
notes.explanation: Power loss rises with resistance, so skin-effect losses grow with frequency too.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 3, copper losses, p. 3-8
notes.evidence: the effective cross-sectional area decreases as the frequency increases. Since resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area, the resistance will increase as the frequency is increased. Also, since power loss increases as resistance increases, power losses increase with an increase in frequency because of skin effect.

notes.front: At {{c1::100 MHz}} or higher, so little current flows in the centre of a wire that the centre could be removed without noticeable effect.
notes.back: 100 MHz
notes.explanation: Current in the centre shrinks as frequency rises, until almost all of it flows on the surface.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 3, copper losses, p. 3-8
notes.evidence: When the frequency applied is 100 megahertz or higher, the electron movement in the center is so small that the center of the wire could be removed without any noticeable effect on current.

notes.front: Reactive power is measured in {{c1::volt-amperes reactive (var)}}, not in watts.
notes.back: volt-amperes reactive (var)
notes.explanation: Watts are kept for real power; the separate unit marks power that is returned to the source.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 2, chapter 4, calculating reactive power, p. 4-20
notes.evidence: The reactive power is the power returned to the source by the reactive components of the circuit. This type of power is measured in Volt-Amperes-Reactive, abbreviated var.

notes.front: A 60-ohm resistor in series with 80 ohms of capacitive reactance draws 0.5 A. How much real power does the circuit use?
notes.choices:
A) 15 W
B) 20 W
C) 25 W
D) 35 W
notes.choicesExplained: B: 20 W is I² × 80, the reactive power, which is returned to the source. C: 25 W uses the whole 100-ohm impedance. D: 35 W adds the reactance as though it were resistance.
notes.explanation: Only the resistance uses power: I²R = 0.5² × 60 = 15 W.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 2, chapter 4, calculating true power, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: This power, measured in watts, is the power associated with the total resistance in the circuit. To calculate true power, the voltage and current associated with the resistance must be used.

notes.front: The same 1-metre coax jumper is used at 1.8 MHz and at 24 GHz. Is it electrically long or short at each?
notes.back: Short at 1.8 MHz (wavelength about 167 m); long at 24 GHz (wavelength about 1.25 cm).
notes.explanation: A quarter-wavelength is about 42 m at 1.8 MHz but about 3 mm at 24 GHz, and 1 metre is judged against that.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 3, length of a transmission line, p. 3-9
notes.evidence: A transmission line is electrically long when its physical length is long compared to a quarter- wavelength of the energy it is to carry. You must understand that the terms "short" and "long" are relative ones.

notes.front: A builder silver-plates the copper tubing of a VHF tank coil. How does that help?
notes.choices:
A) Most of the RF current flows in the silver, a better conductor, cutting copper losses
B) Silver raises the coil's inductance
C) Silver stops the dielectric from heating
D) Silver cancels skin effect entirely
notes.back: Most of the RF current flows in the silver, a better conductor, cutting copper losses
notes.choicesExplained: B: plating does not change the inductance. C: dielectric heating is a separate loss. D: skin effect still happens; it simply happens in better metal.
notes.explanation: Skin effect keeps the current near the surface, so the surface metal decides the loss; the tubing becomes mainly a mechanical support.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 3, copper losses, p. 3-8
notes.evidence: Copper losses can be minimized and conductivity increased in an rf line by plating the line with silver. Since silver is a better conductor than copper, most of the current will flow through the silver layer. The tubing then serves primarily as a mechanical support.

notes.front: At 150 MHz, a copper tube and a solid copper rod have the same outside diameter. Which carries the RF current better?
notes.back: Neither noticeably: at 100 MHz and above so little current flows in the centre that the core could be removed without effect.
notes.explanation: Skin effect has pushed almost all the current into the outer layer, which the tube and the rod share.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 3, copper losses, p. 3-8
notes.evidence: When the frequency applied is 100 megahertz or higher, the electron movement in the center is so small that the center of the wire could be removed without any noticeable effect on current.

notes.front: A coil behaves as an inductor at 3.5 MHz but resonates on its own at a much higher frequency. Which parasitic characteristic is responsible?
notes.choices:
A) Inter-turn capacitance
B) Skin effect
C) Dielectric loss
D) Coupling
notes.back: Inter-turn capacitance
notes.choicesExplained: B: skin effect raises resistance but makes nothing resonate. C: dielectric loss is a capacitor loss. D: coupling links the coil to other coils.
notes.explanation: The capacitance between turns is the parasitic reactance that, with the coil's nominal inductance, gives the self-resonance.
notes.evidence: E5D06 (D) What parasitic characteristic creates an inductor’s self-resonance? A. Skin effect B. Dielectric loss C. Coupling D. Inter-turn capacitance

notes.front: DC versus RF: how is current spread across a wire's cross-section?
notes.back: DC: evenly across the whole cross-section. RF: pushed towards the surface by skin effect.
notes.explanation: With alternating current, the expanding and collapsing fields around each electron retard the electrons they encircle, which the steady DC case lacks.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 3, copper losses, p. 3-7
notes.evidence: When dc flows through a conductor, the movement of electrons through the conductor's cross section is uniform. The situation is somewhat different when ac is applied. The expanding and collapsing fields about each electron encircle other electrons. This phenomenon, called SELF INDUCTION, retards the movement of the encircled electrons.

notes.front: Purely resistive versus purely reactive circuit: what happens to the power in each?
notes.back: Resistive: all of it is consumed, none returned. Reactive: none is consumed, all returned to the source.
notes.explanation: A circuit with both loses some power in its resistance and returns some through its reactance.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 2, chapter 4, power in AC circuits, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: In a purely resistive circuit all of the power is consumed and none is returned to the source; in a purely reactive circuit no power is consumed and all of the power is returned to the source. It follows that in a circuit which contains both resistance and reactance there must be some power dissipated in the resistance

notes.front: What is the result of conductor skin effect?
notes.choices:
A) Resistance increases as frequency increases because RF current flows closer to the surface
B) Resistance decreases as frequency increases because electron mobility increases
C) Resistance increases as temperature increases because of the change in thermal coefficient
D) Resistance decreases as temperature increases because of the change in thermal coefficient
notes.back: Resistance increases as frequency increases because RF current flows closer to the surface
notes.choicesExplained: B: resistance rises, not falls, and electron mobility is not the cause. C and D: skin effect depends on frequency, not on temperature.
notes.explanation: At RF the current crowds towards the surface, shrinking the effective cross-section, and resistance rises as cross-section falls.
notes.evidence: What is the result of conductor skin effect?

notes.front: Why is it important to keep lead lengths short for components used in circuits for VHF and above?
notes.choices:
A) To increase the thermal time constant
B) To minimize inductive reactance
C) To maintain component lifetime
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: To minimize inductive reactance
notes.choicesExplained: A: the thermal time constant is not what lead length is about. C: component lifetime is not the reason given. D: only the inductive reactance answer is right.
notes.explanation: A lead has inductance, and inductive reactance grows with frequency, so at VHF and above even a short lead adds noticeable reactance.
notes.evidence: Why is it important to keep lead lengths short for components used in circuits for VHF and above?

notes.front: What is the phase relationship between current and voltage for reactive power?
notes.choices:
A) They are out of phase
B) They are in phase
C) They are 90 degrees out of phase
D) They are 45 degrees out of phase
notes.back: They are 90 degrees out of phase
notes.choicesExplained: A: too vague; the answer is exactly 90 degrees. B: in phase is the resistor's case, where power is used. D: 45 degrees needs equal resistance and reactance.
notes.explanation: In a reactance the current differs by 90 degrees from the voltage, and power taken in one part of the cycle is returned in the next.
notes.evidence: What is the phase relationship between current and voltage for reactive power?

notes.front: Why are short connections used at microwave frequencies?
notes.choices:
A) To increase neutralizing resistance
B) To reduce phase shift along the connection
C) To increase compensating capacitance
D) To reduce noise figure
notes.back: To reduce phase shift along the connection
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: neutralizing resistance and compensating capacitance are not what short connections are for. D: noise figure is not the reason given.
notes.explanation: At microwaves a connection can be a noticeable part of a wavelength, so extra length delays the signal and shifts its phase.
notes.evidence: Why are short connections used at microwave frequencies?

notes.front: What parasitic characteristic causes electrolytic capacitors to be unsuitable for use at RF?
notes.choices:
A) Skin effect
B) Shunt capacitance
C) Inductance
D) Dielectric leakage
notes.back: Inductance
notes.choicesExplained: A: skin effect is the main RF loss in film capacitors, not what rules out electrolytics. B: shunt capacitance is not the parasitic named. D: dielectric leakage is not the RF problem.
notes.explanation: An electrolytic capacitor's parasitic inductance adds inductive reactance that grows with frequency, working against its capacitance at RF.
notes.evidence: What parasitic characteristic causes electrolytic capacitors to be unsuitable for use at RF?

notes.front: What parasitic characteristic creates an inductor’s self-resonance?
notes.choices:
A) Skin effect
B) Dielectric loss
C) Coupling
D) Inter-turn capacitance
notes.back: Inter-turn capacitance
notes.choicesExplained: A: skin effect raises RF resistance but does not resonate. B: dielectric loss is a capacitor loss. C: coupling links a coil to other coils.
notes.explanation: The capacitance between the turns combines with the coil's own inductance to make a resonant circuit inside the one component.
notes.evidence: What parasitic characteristic creates an inductor’s self-resonance?

notes.front: What combines to create the self-resonance of a component?
notes.choices:
A) The component’s resistance and reactance
B) The component’s nominal and parasitic reactance
C) The component’s inductance and capacitance
D) The component’s electrical length and impedance
notes.back: The component’s nominal and parasitic reactance
notes.choicesExplained: A: resistance does not resonate with reactance. C: too loose; the pool's answer names nominal and parasitic reactance. D: electrical length and impedance do not create self-resonance.
notes.explanation: A real part has its intended (nominal) reactance plus unwanted parasitic reactance, and the two together resonate at some frequency.
notes.evidence: What combines to create the self-resonance of a component?

notes.front: What is the primary cause of loss in film capacitors at RF?
notes.choices:
A) Inductance
B) Dielectric loss
C) Self-discharge
D) Skin effect
notes.back: Skin effect
notes.choicesExplained: A: inductance stores energy rather than losing it. B: dielectric loss is not the pool's primary cause for film capacitors. C: self-discharge is not an RF loss.
notes.explanation: Skin effect raises conductor resistance as frequency rises, and resistance is where power is lost as heat.
notes.evidence: What is the primary cause of loss in film capacitors at RF?

notes.front: What happens to reactive power in ideal inductors and capacitors?
notes.choices:
A) It is dissipated as heat in the circuit
B) Energy is stored in magnetic or electric fields, but power is not dissipated
C) It is canceled by Coulomb forces in the capacitor and inductor
D) It is dissipated in the formation of inductive and capacitive fields
notes.back: Energy is stored in magnetic or electric fields, but power is not dissipated
notes.choicesExplained: A: heat is where real power goes, in resistance. C: Coulomb forces do not cancel it. D: forming the fields stores the energy; it is not dissipated.
notes.explanation: A coil stores energy in its magnetic field and a capacitor in its electric field, then each returns it to the source, so no power is used up.
notes.evidence: What happens to reactive power in ideal inductors and capacitors?

notes.front: As a conductor’s diameter increases, what is the effect on its electrical length?
notes.choices:
A) Thickness has no effect on electrical length
B) It varies randomly
C) It decreases
D) It increases
notes.back: It increases
notes.choicesExplained: A: thickness does change electrical length. B: the change is not random. C: it goes the other way.
notes.explanation: A thicker conductor slows the wave on it: the Army's antenna manual says the wave's velocity falls as the conductor's circumference grows. A slower wave has a shorter wavelength, so a conductor of the same physical length holds more of it and is electrically longer.
notes.evidence: As a conductor’s diameter increases, what is the effect on its electrical length?

notes.front: How much real power is consumed in a circuit consisting of a 100-ohm resistor in series with a 100-ohm inductive reactance drawing 1 ampere?
notes.choices:
A) 70.7 watts
B) 100 watts
C) 141.4 watts
D) 200 watts
notes.back: 100 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A: 70.7 W wrongly applies a 0.707 factor. C: 141.4 W uses the whole impedance, about 141 ohms, instead of the resistance. D: 200 W adds reactance as though it were resistance.
notes.explanation: Real power is used only in the resistance: P = I²R = 1² × 100 = 100 watts. The inductive reactance's share goes back to the source.
notes.evidence: How much real power is consumed in a circuit consisting of a 100-ohm resistor in series with a 100-ohm inductive reactance drawing 1 ampere?

notes.front: What is reactive power?
notes.choices:
A) Power consumed in circuit Q
B) Power consumed by an inductor’s wire resistance
C) The power consumed in inductors and capacitors
D) Wattless, nonproductive power
notes.back: Wattless, nonproductive power
notes.choicesExplained: A: Q is a ratio, not somewhere power is consumed. B: power lost in wire resistance is real power. C: ideal inductors and capacitors consume no power; they store and return it.
notes.explanation: Reactive power flows into a coil or capacitor and back to the source, so it does no work; hence "wattless".
notes.evidence: What is reactive power?
